title: Right action
hookLine: not killing, not stealing, no sexual misconduct (MN 117)
last: ARIYA TUNHIBHAVA — A CHOSEN STILLNESS, SHARED.

lines: THREE ROBES, A BOWL, A RAZOR.
cards: Tradition gives a Buddhist monk a short list of things to own: robes, a bowl, a razor, a needle, a belt. And one more item that's easy to miss: a water strainer, a small cloth for filtering drinking water.
It isn't there for hygiene. It's there so the monk doesn't swallow, and kill, the tiny creatures living in the water.
A whole way of life where even a drink of water is done carefully enough to spare something you can barely see. That's how far one factor of the path reaches.

teach.h: KAMMANTA: THE WORK OF THE BODY.
teach.b: Sammā kammanta. Sammā you know by now: right, whole. Kammanta is action, the work of the body, from the same family as the word kamma.
In the great forty sutta, the Buddha defines it with three abstentions: from killing living beings, from taking what isn't given, and from sexual misconduct.
If those sound familiar, they should: they're the first three of the five precepts, now standing inside the path.
For monks and nuns the third becomes full celibacy; for lay people it means not causing harm through sex, not betraying a partner, not exploiting anyone.
The first sutta of the Long Discourses describes the same ground as a way of living rather than a list of rules.
The Buddha has laid aside the stick and the sword, it says, and lives with care for every living thing, taking only what's given, and waiting for it to be given. That's the shift.
Right action isn't only a fence of not-doing.
It's a way of moving through the world carefully, the way you carry a sleeping child in from the car. Hands that don't grab. Feet that look where they step.

The circle from right speech is here too: right view sees harmful action as harmful, right effort turns away from it, right mindfulness stays awake while it happens. Look back at the week. Four guards.
True, timely, kind. The right time.
Look in the mirror. Not to divide. Speak or be silent.
A whole week on the mouth. Now the body joins in.

how: Lay Buddhists commonly take the five precepts, which include the three abstentions of right action, often reciting them in Pali at the temple; ordained monks and nuns keep a fuller discipline that includes celibacy, and traditionally carry a water strainer among their few requisites.

o: acting without killing, stealing or sexual harm
doing whatever you do with full effort

games.q: what's inside right action: tap the pairs.
p: action, the work of the body

s: right action only asks you to avoid three things
the first sutta of the Long Discourses also describes it positively: stick and sword laid aside, living with care for every being.
a monk's few possessions traditionally include a water strainer
it filters out tiny creatures so they aren't swallowed.
for monks and nuns, the third abstention means celibacy
for lay people it means no sexual misconduct; ordained people give up sex entirely.

games.q: you're a monk on a hot day. the only water nearby is a pond full of tiny living things. what does the monastic life give you for this?
games.why: a water strainer is one of a monk's traditional requisites, so the tiny creatures aren't swallowed. care reaches even a drink of water.

practice: Feel your hands resting, and choose one ordinary action you'll do soon, like making a cup of tea. Rehearse it in your mind, slowly, with great care, how you'll lift, pour, set down, as if everything you touch could feel it.
Then let the hands rest again, and notice how much care they already know how to hold.

wordCard.voice: Sammā kammanta. Right action: not killing, not taking what isn't given, no sexual misconduct. The fourth factor of the path.

orig.note: Pali sammā kammanta: right action, the fourth factor of the eightfold path.

carryVoice: Your line: act with care. Hands that don't grab, feet that look where they step. And that's another week.
